teach.what: A mudslide buried a sea floor so fast that soft bodies, including legs, guts, and eyes, turned to stone. The fossil is Anomalocaris, a top predator. The drawing is five-eyed Opabinia, a different animal from these rocks.
teach.when: About 508 million years ago, in the Middle Cambrian, when animals were brand-new.
teach.where: High in the Rocky Mountains of Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada.
teach.why: It is one of the best snapshots of the Cambrian explosion, when most animal body plans first appeared.

learnMore.label: Royal Ontario Museum: The Burgess Shale
UNESCO World Heritage: Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks (includes the Burgess Shale)

specimen.alt: Fossil of Anomalocaris canadensis, a Burgess Shale predator. This photo may show a museum cast.
specimen.credit: Esv, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. May be a museum cast.
specimen.caption: Anomalocaris canadensis

restoration.alt: Life restoration of Opabinia regalis, a five-eyed animal from the Burgess Shale. This is not the same animal as the Anomalocaris fossil.
restoration.credit: Nobu Tamura, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.
restoration.caption: Opabinia regalis

teach.what: Animals that sank into a deep volcanic lake were preserved whole, with skin, feathers, fur outlines, and even last meals. The fossil is Darwinius, nicknamed Ida. The model is Propalaeotherium, an early horse from the same pit, not the same animal.
teach.when: About 48 million years ago, in the Middle Eocene.
teach.where: The Messel Pit, near Frankfurt in Hesse, Germany.
teach.why: It shows the early days of modern mammals after the dinosaurs, including tiny early horses and some of the first bats. More than 1,000 species of plants and animals have been found here.

learnMore.label: UNESCO World Heritage: Messel Pit Fossil Site

specimen.alt: Fossil of Darwinius masillae, the primate nicknamed Ida, from the Messel Pit.
specimen.credit: Jens L. Franzen, Philip D. Gingerich, Jörg Habersetzer, Jørn H. Hurum, Wighart von Koenigswald, and B. Holly Smith, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
specimen.caption: Darwinius masillae (Ida)

restoration.alt: Model of Propalaeotherium, an early horse, at the Messel Pit. This is not the same animal as the Darwinius fossil.
restoration.credit: Fritz Geller-Grimm; derivative work by Xvazquez, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons. Photo of a model.
restoration.caption: Propalaeotherium (early horse)

teach.what: Rivers buried dinosaurs in sand and mud on a warm coastal plain. Wind and rain now uncover them in the badlands. The skeleton is Gorgosaurus, a tyrannosaur. The drawing is Centrosaurus, a horned dinosaur. They are different animals from this park.
teach.when: 75 to 77 million years ago, in the Late Cretaceous.
teach.where: Dinosaur Provincial Park, Alberta, Canada.
teach.why: More than 44 dinosaur species and more than 350 articulated skeletons have been found here. It is one of the richest places to see who lived together in the last chapter of the dinosaurs.

learnMore.label: UNESCO World Heritage: Dinosaur Provincial Park

specimen.alt: Skeleton of Gorgosaurus libratus, a tyrannosaur from the Dinosaur Park Formation, at the Royal Tyrrell Museum.
specimen.credit: IJReid, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
specimen.caption: Gorgosaurus libratus

restoration.alt: Life restoration of Centrosaurus, a horned dinosaur from Dinosaur Provincial Park. This is not the same animal as the Gorgosaurus skeleton.
restoration.credit: LadyofHats, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.
restoration.caption: Centrosaurus

sites.n: La Brea Tar Pits, Los Angeles, USA

teach.what: Sticky asphalt trapped Ice Age animals and preserved their bones, including saber-toothed cats, dire wolves, mammoths, and giant ground sloths. Both pictures are a saber-toothed cat (Smilodon).
teach.when: The last ice age, from about 50,000 to 10,000 years ago.
teach.where: The La Brea Tar Pits, in Los Angeles, California, USA.
teach.why: It is the world’s richest Ice Age fossil site in a city. Scientists still dig here in public view, and the bones show how animals and climate changed as people arrived.

specimen.alt: Skeleton of a saber-toothed cat (Smilodon).
specimen.credit: TheUltimateGrass, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
specimen.caption: Saber-toothed cat (Smilodon)

restoration.alt: Charles R. Knight painting of a saber-toothed cat (Smilodon).
restoration.credit: Charles Robert Knight, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.
restoration.caption: Saber-toothed cat (Smilodon)

teach.what: Before animals had shells, bones, or legs, the sea floor was covered in soft creatures shaped like discs, fronds, and ribbons. The fossil is Dickinsonia costata, from these hills. The drawing is Dickinsonia menneri, a related species.
teach.when: About 560 to 542 million years ago, in the Ediacaran Period. Reg Sprigg found the imprints here in 1946, and that age is named after these hills.
teach.where: The Ediacara Hills in the Flinders Ranges, at Nilpena Ediacara National Park, South Australia.
teach.why: It is the dawn of animal life. Dickinsonia is among the oldest known animals, and tiny Ikaria may be an early ancestor of animals with a left and right side, like us. The Flinders Ranges are on UNESCO’s Tentative List (a nomination was submitted in 2026). They are not a World Heritage site yet.

learnMore.label: UNESCO Tentative List: Flinders Ranges (not inscribed yet)

specimen.alt: Fossil of Dickinsonia costata, a soft-bodied animal from the Ediacara Hills.
specimen.credit: Verisimilus at English Wikipedia, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
specimen.caption: Dickinsonia costata

restoration.alt: Life restoration of Dickinsonia menneri, a related species, shown alive. This is not the same species as the Dickinsonia costata fossil.
restoration.credit: Apokryltaros, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.
restoration.caption: Dickinsonia menneri

teach.what: Whole skeletons of early whales, still with tiny back legs and feet. The photo is a Basilosaurus isis jaw in the rock. The drawing is Basilosaurus cetoides, a related species.
teach.when: About 40 to 37 million years ago, in the Late Eocene.
teach.where: Wadi Al-Hitan, Whale Valley, in the Fayoum, Egypt. This desert was a shallow sea then.
teach.why: Whales used to walk. This is the most important place to see them changing from land animals into ocean swimmers. The rocks also hold Dorudon.

learnMore.label: UNESCO World Heritage: Wadi Al-Hitan (Whale Valley)

specimen.alt: Lower jaw of Basilosaurus isis, photographed in place at Wadi Al-Hitan.
specimen.credit: Tom Horton, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
specimen.caption: Basilosaurus isis

restoration.alt: Life restoration of Basilosaurus cetoides, a long-bodied early whale with tiny hind legs. This is a related species, not the Basilosaurus isis jaw beside it.
restoration.credit: Connor Ashbridge, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.
restoration.caption: Basilosaurus cetoides

teach.what: These rocks record the Triassic, when the first dinosaurs and the first mammal relatives appeared. The pictures are Eoraptor, a small early meat-eater. The skull is a museum cast, not the original fossil.
teach.when: About 231 to 225 million years ago, in the Late Triassic. The valley’s rocks span much of the Triassic, about 250 to 200 million years ago.
teach.where: Ischigualasto Provincial Park, the Valley of the Moon, in San Juan, Argentina.
teach.why: It is the opening scene of the Age of Dinosaurs. Early meat-eaters such as Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus were found here.

learnMore.label: UNESCO World Heritage: Ischigualasto / Talampaya Natural Parks

specimen.alt: Cast of an Eoraptor skull, one of the first dinosaurs, from Ischigualasto. This is not the original fossil.
specimen.credit: Ghedoghedo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Museum cast, not the original fossil.
specimen.caption: Eoraptor skull (cast)

restoration.alt: Life restoration of Eoraptor lunensis, an early dinosaur from Ischigualasto.
restoration.credit: Ildarotyrannus, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.
restoration.caption: Eoraptor lunensis

teach.what: Sea reptiles, fish, ammonites, and shrimp-like animals sank into a calm tropical lagoon. The pictures are Tanystropheus, a reptile with a neck longer than its body.
teach.when: 245 to 230 million years ago, in the Middle Triassic.
teach.where: Monte San Giorgio, by Lake Lugano, on the border of Ticino, Switzerland, and Lombardy, Italy.
teach.why: It is the best-known record of ocean life from the Triassic, just after Earth’s biggest mass extinction.

learnMore.label: UNESCO World Heritage: Monte San Giorgio

specimen.alt: Fossil of Tanystropheus longobardicus, a long-necked reptile from Monte San Giorgio.
specimen.credit: Ghedoghedo, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

restoration.alt: Life restoration of Tanystropheus, a reptile whose neck is longer than its body.
restoration.credit: Nobu Tamura, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.

teach.what: Some of the oldest large, complex animal-like life ever found. These are soft, frond-shaped seafloor creatures pressed into rock.
teach.when: 580–560 million years ago, in the Ediacaran Period, before animals had shells or bones.
teach.where: Sea cliffs at Mistaken Point, on Newfoundland’s southeastern tip, Canada.
teach.why: It shows life getting big for the first time, in a deep ocean. Volcanic ash buried the seafloor and kept the shapes.

specimen.alt: Fossil fronds on a rock surface at Mistaken Point, Newfoundland, with a coin for scale
specimen.credit: Alicejmichel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

restoration.alt: Life restoration of Fractofusus misrai, a soft-bodied creature from Mistaken Point
restoration.credit: Oleg Kuznetsov (3D Epix), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.

teach.what: Animals preserved in amazing detail, sometimes including soft body parts. The pictures are Fuxianhuia protensa, an arthropod from this site.
teach.when: About 530 million years ago, during the Cambrian explosion.
teach.where: Yunnan Province, China.
teach.why: Almost all of today’s major animal groups got their start in this short burst of time.

learnMore.label: UNESCO World Heritage: Chengjiang Fossil Site

specimen.alt: Fossil of Fuxianhuia protensa from the Chengjiang biota
specimen.credit: Woudloper, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

restoration.alt: Life restoration of Fuxianhuia protensa, an adult and three young
restoration.credit: Junnn11, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.

sites.n: Joggins Fossil Cliffs, Nova Scotia, Canada

teach.what: Whole fossil trees still stand upright in the cliffs, and some of the earliest reptiles were preserved inside hollow trunks.
teach.when: The Coal Age (Carboniferous), about 300 million years ago. UNESCO dates these rock layers to 318–303 million years ago.
teach.where: The Bay of Fundy shore at Joggins, Nova Scotia, Canada.
teach.why: Swamp forests like these became much of the world’s coal, which ties this cliff to the climate story. UNESCO and Parks Canada call the reptiles here the earliest amniotes in these rocks.

learnMore.label: UNESCO World Heritage: Joggins Fossil Cliffs

specimen.alt: Upright fossil tree trunk in the cliff at Joggins Fossil Cliffs, Nova Scotia
specimen.credit: Michael C. Rygel, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

restoration.alt: Life restoration of Hylonomus lyelli, an early reptile from Joggins
restoration.credit: Nobu Tamura, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.

sites.n: Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, USA

teach.what: Logs that slowly turned into colorful stone (quartz), along with early dinosaurs and their relatives. The drawing is Chindesaurus, an early dinosaur found in this park.
teach.when: Late Triassic, more than 200 million years ago.
teach.where: Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, USA.
teach.why: It records life on land after the greatest extinction of all time, when forests and early dinosaurs shared a river plain.

learnMore.label: National Park Service: dinosaurs of Petrified Forest

specimen.alt: Colorful petrified log at Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona
specimen.credit: Moondigger, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

restoration.alt: Life restoration of Chindesaurus, an early dinosaur from Petrified Forest, in a forest
restoration.credit: Petrified Forest National Park staff, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.

teach.what: A rock wall in the Quarry Exhibit Hall still holds about 1,500 dinosaur bones. The National Park Service names Allosaurus, Apatosaurus, Camarasaurus, Diplodocus, and Stegosaurus among them.
teach.when: Late Jurassic, about 150 million years ago.
teach.where: Dinosaur National Monument, on the Utah–Colorado border, USA.
teach.why: It shows an ancient river ecosystem and how the animals were buried together in the Morrison Formation.

learnMore.label: National Park Service: Quarry Exhibit Hall

specimen.alt: Wall of dinosaur bones still in the rock at Dinosaur National Monument
specimen.credit: Drake411, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

restoration.alt: Life restoration of Allosaurus, a dinosaur whose bones are in this quarry wall
restoration.credit: Nobu Tamura, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.

teach.what: 155 km of coastline whose rock layers hold about 185 million years of Earth history, including marine reptiles such as Ichthyosaurus from Lyme Regis.
teach.when: Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous time, stacked in one coast.
teach.where: The Dorset and East Devon coast, England.
teach.why: The coast keeps eroding, so new fossils keep appearing. People have studied these cliffs for over 300 years.

learnMore.label: UNESCO World Heritage: Dorset and East Devon Coast

specimen.alt: Skull of Ichthyosaurus communis from Lyme Regis on the Jurassic Coast
specimen.credit: James St. John, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Specimen at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History.

restoration.alt: Life restoration of Ichthyosaurus communis
restoration.credit: Nobu Tamura, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.

teach.what: Fossils of ancient marsupials. The pictures are Nimbadon lavarackorum, a wombat relative from Riversleigh. Naracoorte’s caves also hold ice-age animals, including the marsupial lion.
teach.when: The last tens of millions of years. Riversleigh’s mammals are about 30 to 10 million years old. Naracoorte records a later ice age.
teach.where: Riversleigh in Queensland and Naracoorte in South Australia. This pin sits at Riversleigh.
teach.why: Australia was almost on its own for about 35 million years after it split from Antarctica, so its mammals became unique as habitats changed.

learnMore.label: UNESCO World Heritage: Australian Fossil Mammal Sites

specimen.alt: Skeleton of Nimbadon lavarackorum from Riversleigh, Australia
specimen.credit: Black, Camens, Archer, and Hand, PLOS ONE (2012), CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

restoration.alt: Life restoration of Nimbadon lavarackorum, a wombat relative, with a young one in a tree
restoration.credit: Peter Schouten, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.

teach.what: Caves full of fossils of early human relatives, including the Taung Child, a young Australopithecus africanus.
teach.when: From more than 3.5 million years ago up toward the recent past.
teach.where: Sterkfontein, Swartkrans, Kromdraai, the Makapan Valley, and Taung, South Africa.
teach.why: It is a main record of how our own family tree changed across more than 3.5 million years.

learnMore.label: UNESCO World Heritage: Fossil Hominid Sites of South Africa

specimen.alt: Cast of the Taung Child, Australopithecus africanus, with the natural brain cast still attached
specimen.credit: Didier Descouens, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Museum cast, not the original fossil.

restoration.alt: Life restoration of the Taung Child’s face. This is a model, not a photograph.
restoration.credit: Cicero Moraes and colleagues, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Life restoration, not a photograph.

sites.n: EPICA Dome C & Vostok ice cores, Antarctica

teach.what: Snow that falls in Antarctica never melts. It piles up and squeezes into ice, trapping tiny bubbles of real ancient air. Scientists drilled more than 3 km down at Dome C (EPICA) and Vostok.
teach.when: The ice goes back about 800,000 years, through eight ice-age cycles, and up to today.
teach.where: Dome C (EPICA) and Vostok, in East Antarctica. This pin sits at Dome C.
teach.why: Those bubbles show that carbon dioxide and temperature rose and fell together through eight ice-age cycles. It is a direct sample of Earth’s old sky.

specimen.alt: Thin slice of Antarctic ice under polarized light, crowded with tiny bubbles of trapped air.
specimen.credit: CSIRO, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. A slice of Antarctic ice, not the Dome C or Vostok core.
specimen.label: Ice

restoration.alt: Diagram of temperature and carbon dioxide from the EPICA Dome C and Vostok ice cores over about 800,000 years.
restoration.credit: Leland McInnes, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
restoration.label: Diagram

teach.what: On top of Greenland, each year’s snow makes a thin layer, like tree rings made of ice. Drilling projects GISP2 and NGRIP counted and measured those layers.
teach.when: From the last warm period, about 123,000 years ago, through today.
teach.where: GISP2, on the Greenland ice sheet. NGRIP is another Greenland drill site from the same kind of work. This pin sits at GISP2.
teach.why: They showed that climate can flip suddenly. Big warmings happened in just decades, not only slowly.

specimen.alt: Section of the GISP2 ice core from Greenland, lit from below so the yearly light and dark layers show.
specimen.credit: NOAA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
specimen.label: Ice core

restoration.alt: Diagram of temperature changes recorded in the GISP2 ice core, with sharp warm and cold swings.
restoration.credit: Xavax, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Based on Alley (2000).
restoration.label: Diagram

sites.n: Hamersley banded iron, Karijini NP, Western Australia

teach.what: These gorge walls are striped red and grey, layer after layer. The red stripes are iron rust that settled on an ancient sea floor when tiny microbes started making oxygen, and that oxygen rusted iron dissolved in the ocean.
teach.when: About 2.5 billion years ago.
teach.where: The Hamersley Range, in Karijini National Park, Western Australia.
teach.why: It is a record of the Great Oxidation, the time life began filling the air with the oxygen we breathe.

specimen.alt: Banded iron formation in the Hamersley Range, with red and grey stripes.
specimen.credit: U.S. Geological Survey, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
specimen.label: Rock

restoration.alt: Diagram of oxygen building up in Earth’s air. One stage marks iron-rust bands on the seafloor.
restoration.credit: Tameeria, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Simplified diagram. The middle stage is iron-rust bands on the seafloor.
restoration.label: Diagram

sites.n: Shark Bay stromatolites (Hamelin Pool), Western Australia

teach.what: These lumpy rocks in shallow, extra-salty water are alive. Sticky mats of microbes trap sand and grow upward.
teach.when: They are living today. Rocks like these are among the oldest signs of life on Earth, over 3 billion years old.
teach.where: Hamelin Pool, in Shark Bay, Western Australia.
teach.why: Hamelin Pool lets you see today what Earth’s earliest life-built structures looked like. It is a living time machine.

specimen.alt: Lumpy living stromatolites in the shallow water of Hamelin Pool, Shark Bay.
specimen.credit: Bryn Pinzgauer, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
specimen.label: Rock

restoration.alt: Stromatolites on the seafloor at Shark Bay, seen from underwater, with a snorkeler near the surface.
restoration.credit: Ed Landing and Markes E. Johnson, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
restoration.label: Underwater

teach.what: Inside these hills are crystals smaller than a grain of sand, called zircons. One was dated to about 4.4 billion years, Earth’s oldest known piece.
teach.when: About 4.4 billion years ago, when the planet was only about 150 million years old.
teach.where: The Jack Hills, Western Australia.
teach.why: Its chemistry hints that Earth already had continental crust and liquid water oceans very early, far sooner than people expected.

specimen.alt: Polished quartz-pebble metaconglomerate from the Jack Hills. Zircon grains older than 4 billion years come from this kind of rock.
specimen.credit: James St. John, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
specimen.label: Rock

restoration.alt: Artist’s illustration of a fiery early Earth. This is not a photograph of the Jack Hills, and it does not show the oceans the zircons suggest.
restoration.credit: Tim Bertelink, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.
restoration.label: Restoration

teach.what: These mountains hold some of the best-kept rocks from early Earth: old volcanoes, sea floor, and even layers of droplets from giant meteorite impacts.
teach.when: 3.6 to 3.25 billion years ago.
teach.where: The Barberton Makhonjwa Mountains, South Africa.
teach.why: It is one of the clearest windows on young Earth, when continents were first forming and early life was just getting started (UNESCO).

learnMore.label: UNESCO World Heritage: Barberton Makhonjwa Mountains

specimen.alt: Ancient volcanic rock with a spinifex texture, from the Komati River valley in the Barberton mountains.
specimen.credit: James St. John, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
specimen.label: Rock

restoration.alt: Satellite view of the Barberton Makhonjwa Mountains in South Africa.
restoration.credit: NASA / Jesse Allen, using Landsat data, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
restoration.label: Landscape

teach.what: In a roadside cliff near Gubbio there is a thin clay layer between two kinds of limestone. In 1980 the Alvarez team found it full of iridium, a metal rare on Earth but common in asteroids.
teach.when: About 66 million years ago.
teach.where: Bottaccione Gorge, near Gubbio, Italy.
teach.why: It was the first big clue that an asteroid hit Earth 66 million years ago and helped end the dinosaurs. The crater was later found at Chicxulub, Mexico.

specimen.alt: The thin clay layer at the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary in the roadside cliff at Gubbio, Italy.
specimen.credit: Biandh, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
specimen.label: Cliff

restoration.alt: Artist’s illustration of the Chicxulub asteroid impact. This is not a photograph.
restoration.credit: Donald E. Davis, NASA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.
restoration.label: Restoration

sites.n: Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona, USA

teach.what: The Colorado River cut a mile-deep slice through Arizona, so you can see rock layers stacked like pages in a book. The oldest at the bottom are nearly 2 billion years old. Younger layers above record old seas, deserts, and swamps (NPS).
teach.when: About 1.8 billion years of rock, from nearly 2 billion years ago up through much younger layers.
teach.where: Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona, USA.
teach.why: It is one of the easiest places on Earth to see deep time with your own eyes.

specimen.alt: Grand Canyon cliffs, with flat rock layers stacked above the river.
specimen.credit: Mx. Granger, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.
specimen.label: Canyon

restoration.alt: National Park Service diagram of the stacked rock layers in the Grand Canyon, cut by the Colorado River.
restoration.credit: National Park Service, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
restoration.label: Diagram

teach.what: On a small island in a remote Canadian river sits some of the oldest rock on Earth — a striped stone called gneiss, about 4.03 billion years old. Scientists dated tiny zircon crystals inside it (Bowring & Williams, 1999).
teach.when: About 4.03 billion years ago, when Earth was less than 600 million years old.
teach.where: A small island in a remote river in the Northwest Territories, Canada.
teach.why: It is a real piece of Earth’s very first crust — the oldest whole rock you can stand on.

specimen.alt: Striped fragment of Acasta gneiss on a museum stand. This piece is on display in Vienna, not the island outcrop.
specimen.credit: Pedroalexandrade, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Museum specimen at the Natural History Museum in Vienna, not the island outcrop.
specimen.label: Rock
specimen.caption: Acasta gneiss (museum piece)

restoration.alt: Artist’s concept of early Earth: a dark beach, lightning, an erupting volcano, and a meteor. Not a photograph.
restoration.credit: NASA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s concept.
restoration.label: Artist’s concept
restoration.caption: Artist’s concept of early Earth, not a photograph and not the Acasta island.

sites.n: Snowball Earth glacial & cap-carbonate rocks, Otavi Mountains, Namibia

teach.what: In northern Namibia, rocks dropped by glaciers sit right under thick pink limestone that forms in warm seas. Paul Hoffman’s team (1998) argued the whole planet froze over — ice nearly to the equator — and then flipped to a hothouse when volcanoes built up enough carbon dioxide.
teach.when: About 717 to 635 million years ago.
teach.where: The Otavi Mountains, northern Namibia.
teach.why: Earth has nearly frozen solid and recovered, and complex animal life showed up soon after.

specimen.alt: National Science Foundation diagram showing ice reaching low latitudes, then a warm ice-free world, from about 716 to 630 million years ago.
specimen.credit: National Science Foundation, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Diagram of the idea, not a photograph of Namibia.
specimen.label: Diagram
specimen.caption: A drawing of the snowball idea, not the Otavi rocks.

restoration.alt: Artist’s concept of a cracked, ice-covered world in space. Not a photograph of Earth and not a scientific reconstruction of Snowball Earth.
restoration.credit: Pablo Carlos Budassi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s concept.
restoration.label: Artist’s concept
restoration.caption: Artist’s concept of an ice-covered world, not a photograph of Earth.

sites.n: Elatina Formation tillite, Flinders Ranges, South Australia

teach.what: This jumbled rock is old glacier rubble — boulders and mud dumped by ice. Magnetic clues show it formed close to the equator.
teach.when: About 640 to 635 million years ago.
teach.where: The Elatina Formation, in the Flinders Ranges, South Australia.
teach.why: If glaciers reached sea level near the equator, ice must have covered most of Earth. It is one of the best pieces of evidence for Snowball Earth, just below the rocks where the Ediacaran period officially begins.

specimen.alt: Reddish rock full of pebbles and mud, the Elatina Formation tillite at Enorama Creek in the Flinders Ranges.
specimen.credit: James St. John, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
specimen.label: Rock
specimen.caption: Elatina tillite, Enorama Creek

restoration.alt: Artist’s concept of a cracked, ice-covered world in space. Not a photograph of the Flinders Ranges.
restoration.credit: Pablo Carlos Budassi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s concept.
restoration.label: Artist’s concept
restoration.caption: Artist’s concept of an ice-covered world, not a photograph of Earth.

teach.what: Buried under Mexico’s Yucatán is a crater about 180 km wide, made when an asteroid roughly 10 km across hit Earth. It was identified in 1991 (Hildebrand et al.), solving the mystery that started with the iridium clay at Gubbio, Italy.
teach.when: About 66 million years ago.
teach.where: Under the Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico.
teach.why: The blast and the years of darkness after it ended the age of dinosaurs and opened the world for mammals — including us.

learnMore.label: NASA Earth Observatory: Yucatán relief map

specimen.alt: NASA radar map of the Yucatán Peninsula. A dashed arc marks a shallow trough and sinkholes along the buried Chicxulub crater’s rim.
specimen.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Shuttle Radar Topography Mission.
specimen.label: Map
specimen.caption: Radar map of the buried crater’s rim

restoration.alt: Painting of a huge asteroid hitting Earth, with flying reptiles and streaks of debris. Artist’s concept, not a photograph.
restoration.credit: Donald E. Davis, NASA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s concept.

teach.what: In a steep Scottish gully, dark shale is packed with graptolites — tiny floating sea animals that look like pencil marks or saw blades.
teach.when: Around 445 to 443 million years ago, at the end of the Ordovician. A short ice age gripped the planet and sea levels dropped.
teach.where: Dob’s Linn, near Moffat, Scotland. Geologists picked this gully as the world’s official marker for where the Silurian begins.
teach.why: About 85% of ocean species vanished in the first of the Big Five mass extinctions. The ocean’s tiny drifters show how fast life can crash — and come back.

learnMore.label: Global boundary markers (International Commission on Stratigraphy)

sites.n: Coumiac Quarry (Frasnian–Famennian boundary), Montagne Noire, France

teach.what: This old red-marble quarry in southern France holds the world’s official marker for the Late Devonian extinction (Klapper et al., 1993).
teach.when: About 372 million years ago, in the Late Devonian.
teach.where: Coumiac Quarry, in the Montagne Noire of southern France.
teach.why: Giant armored fish like Dunkleosteus ruled the seas, and reefs were bigger than today’s Great Barrier Reef. Then oceans lost oxygen in pulses, and reef-builders and many fish were wiped out. Reefs took millions of years to recover. It is a warning from the past about what low-oxygen oceans do to reefs.

specimen.alt: The red rock wall of Coumiac Quarry, with a wooden fence along the path.
specimen.credit: Guillaume « Frozman » Calas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
specimen.caption: Red marble wall at Coumiac Quarry
specimen.label: Quarry

restoration.alt: Artist’s concept of Dunkleosteus, a giant armored fish from Late Devonian seas. This is period life, not a fossil found at Coumiac.
restoration.credit: PlacodermReconstructions, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s concept.
restoration.caption: Late Devonian ocean life. Artist’s concept of Dunkleosteus, a giant armored fish. Not a fossil from Coumiac.

teach.what: These huge flat-topped mountains are made of lava — stack after stack of it, covering an area bigger than western Europe.
teach.when: About 252 million years ago, right around the Great Dying.
teach.where: The Siberian Traps, on the Putorana Plateau in Russia. This pin sits on the plateau. The cliff photo is at Krasnye Kamni, near Norilsk, in the same lava province.
teach.why: The eruptions pumped out carbon dioxide and other gases that heated the planet and soured the oceans (Burgess and Bowring, 2015). It is the leading suspect for Earth’s worst extinction — a natural experiment in what huge amounts of CO2 can do.

learnMore.label: Timing of the eruptions (Burgess and Bowring, 2015)

sites.n: Karoo Basin (Lystrosaurus beds), Eastern Cape, South Africa

teach.what: The dry Karoo has rock layers that run straight through the Great Dying on land. Below the line lived many kinds of strange reptile-like ancestors of mammals. Above it, almost everywhere you dig, one animal turns up: Lystrosaurus, a pig-sized plant-eater with two tusks and a beak.
teach.when: About 252 to 250 million years ago, right after the end-Permian extinction.
teach.where: The Karoo Basin, Eastern Cape, South Africa.
teach.why: After a disaster, a few tough survivors can take over the whole world. Lystrosaurus is our distant cousin on the mammal side of the family tree (Smith and Ward, 2001).

specimen.alt: Skull of Lystrosaurus murrayi on a museum shelf. The label says the fossil is from Thaba Nchu, South Africa.
specimen.credit: Ghedoghedo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
specimen.caption: Lystrosaurus murrayi skull

restoration.caption: Artist’s concept of Lystrosaurus (the big plant-eaters) and crocodile-like Proterosuchus. Not a photograph of the Karoo.

sites.n: Palisades Sill (CAMP lavas), New Jersey, USA

teach.what: The tall cliffs across the Hudson River from New York City are cooled magma. They formed when the supercontinent Pangaea began tearing apart to make the Atlantic Ocean.
teach.when: About 201 million years ago, at the end of the Triassic.
teach.where: The Palisades, along the Hudson River in New Jersey, USA. This pin is those cliffs. Dinosaur footprints in the Connecticut Valley are about 200 km northeast, in Massachusetts.
teach.why: Those eruptions, the CAMP, line up in time with the end-Triassic extinction (Blackburn et al., 2013). Rocks in the Connecticut Valley keep dinosaur footprints that get bigger right after the extinction. You can see the cause of a mass extinction from a New York highway.

learnMore.label: CAMP and the end-Triassic (Blackburn et al., 2013)

specimen.alt: The Palisades, a tall dark cliff of cooled magma above trees, with the Hudson River beyond.
specimen.credit: CrankyScorpion, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
specimen.caption: The Palisades cliffs above the Hudson River
specimen.label: Cliff

restoration.alt: Artist’s concept of Dilophosaurus, a crested early dinosaur, sitting and leaving footprints. A Dilophosaurus-like animal may have made Connecticut Valley tracks. This drawing is not the Palisades and not a fossil from New Jersey.
restoration.credit: Heather Kyoht Luterman, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s concept.

sites.n: Deccan Traps, Western Ghats, Maharashtra, India

teach.what: The step-shaped hills of western India are giant lava flows that erupted in pulses around the time the dinosaurs died.
teach.when: About 66 million years ago, at the end of the Cretaceous.
teach.where: The Deccan Traps, in the Western Ghats of Maharashtra, India.
teach.why: Two teams in 2019 (Schoene et al.; Sprain et al.) dated the lava and still debate how much it helped the Chicxulub asteroid end the dinosaurs. Real science has open questions. Open the Gubbio coin for the iridium clue. Its See also button flies to the Chicxulub coin.

learnMore.label: Lava dates, team one (Schoene et al., 2019)
Lava dates, team two (Sprain et al., 2019)

specimen.label: Hills

teach.what: Near the village of Rhynie, hot springs once bubbled like Yellowstone’s. Their silica-rich water flooded a marsh and turned it to glassy stone so fast that tiny plants, fungi, and bugs were frozen cell by cell. The rock shows Horneophyton. The drawing is Aglaophyton, a different plant from the same marsh. These plants were ankle-high, with no leaves and no roots like ours — just green stems.
teach.when: About 410 million years ago, in the Early Devonian. The University of Aberdeen also rounds this rock to about 400 million years old.
teach.where: Near Rhynie, in Aberdeenshire, Scotland.
teach.why: It is the best snapshot of the very first land ecosystems, when green life was just leaving the water.

learnMore.label: University of Aberdeen: The Rhynie Chert

teach.what: In Victoria’s hills, the rocks hold Baragwanathia, a clubmoss with tiny needle-like leaves. It looks like a green pipe cleaner. Both rounds are fossils of that plant. The second photo is another specimen in a museum, not a drawing of it alive.
teach.when: More than 410 million years ago. Museums Victoria calls the Yea rocks Early Devonian. Other scientists think they may be a little older, from the very end of the Silurian. The exact age is still debated.
teach.where: Near Yea, in Victoria, Australia. Back then this land was part of the supercontinent Gondwana.
teach.why: It is one of the oldest plants with real leaves and veins to carry water. Those veins were the plumbing that later let plants grow tall.

specimen.caption: Baragwanathia longifolia from the Yea beds, Victoria

sites.n: Gilboa Fossil Forest (and nearby Cairo forest), New York, USA

teach.what: Workers digging a dam in 1870 found stone tree stumps from one of Earth’s earliest forests. The trees, called Wattieza or Eospermatopteris, looked like giant palm-shaped feather dusters, at least 8 metres tall, but they made spores, not seeds. A nearby quarry at Cairo, New York, holds even older roots.
teach.when: About 385 million years ago, in the Middle Devonian. The Cairo roots are a little older, about 386 million years.
teach.where: Gilboa, in Schoharie County, New York, USA. This pin sits at Gilboa. Cairo is a nearby quarry.
teach.why: The first forests pulled carbon out of the air and changed Earth’s climate.

specimen.alt: Fossil tree stump of Eospermatopteris from Riverside Quarry at Gilboa, New York, on display at the Field Museum.
specimen.credit: James St. John, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
specimen.caption: Eospermatopteris stump from Gilboa, on display at the Field Museum
specimen.label: Stump

sites.n: Kiltorcan Old Quarry, County Kilkenny, Ireland

teach.what: Yellow sandstone at Kiltorcan holds fronds of Archaeopteris hibernica. The photo is a fossil frond of that species, on display in a museum. The drawing shows a related species, Archaeopteris macilenta, from New York, so you can picture the whole tree. It is an artist’s concept, not a photograph, and it is not the Irish fossil.
teach.when: Latest Devonian, about 360 million years ago, near the end of that period. Geological Survey Ireland dates the quarry’s rock to the latest Devonian.
teach.where: Kiltorcan Old Quarry, on Kiltorcan Hill near Ballyhale, County Kilkenny, Ireland. The quarry is on private land.
teach.why: Archaeopteris is sometimes called the first modern tree: a woody trunk, wide branches, and flat fronds, but it shed spores instead of seeds. That idea comes from how the tree grew, studied in fossils from Morocco, not from this one frond. Forests of it spread worldwide. Deep roots broke rock into soil, and woody trees locked carbon away, which helped cool the planet.

learnMore.label: Geological Survey Ireland: Kiltorcan Old Quarry

sites.n: Fossil Grove, Victoria Park, Glasgow, Scotland, UK

teach.what: In a Glasgow park, 11 stone tree stumps still stand exactly where they grew. They were scale trees, Lepidodendron — giant clubmosses with bark like snake skin. The drawing is an artist’s concept of the whole tree, not a photo of this park.
teach.when: About 330 million years ago, in the Carboniferous, the Coal Age.
teach.where: Fossil Grove, in Victoria Park, Glasgow, Scotland. Back then this place was a steamy swamp near the equator. Scotland has drifted north since. The stumps were found in 1887 and have been kept under a roof ever since. Glasgow City Council owns the site.
teach.why: Forests like this became the coal that powered the Industrial Revolution.

specimen.alt: Stone tree stumps standing where they grew inside the Fossil Grove building in Victoria Park, Glasgow.
specimen.credit: Richard Sutcliffe, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (geograph.org.uk).

specimen.label: Stumps

teach.what: Explorers on Scott’s 1912 expedition hauled Glossopteris leaf fossils off Antarctic rock. The photo is a tongue-shaped leaf from Antarctic rock in a museum, not one of those original samples. The other round is a map of where the same kind of leaf turns up, not a drawing of the living tree.
teach.when: About 270 to 252 million years ago, in the Permian, when Antarctica was warmer.
teach.where: The Transantarctic Mountains. This pin marks that mountain region, not one exact cliff. The same leaves are also found in India, Africa, South America, and Australia.
teach.why: A leaf helped show that those lands were once joined in the supercontinent Gondwana, and that continents move. It also shows that Antarctica once had forests.

specimen.alt: Tongue-shaped Glossopteris leaf from Permian rocks of Antarctica, on display at Ohio State University. This is not one of Scott’s original samples.
specimen.credit: James St. John, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
specimen.caption: Glossopteris leaf from Permian rocks of Antarctica, on display at Ohio State University. Not one of Scott’s samples.
